authors: Lois M. Davis, Robert Bozick, Jennifer L. Steele, Jessica Saunders, Jeremy N. V. Miles
title: Evaluating the Effectiveness of Correctional Education: A Meta-Analysis of Programs That Provide Education to Incarcerated Adults
key_finding: Comprehensive meta-analysis: correctional education while incarcerated reduces inmates' risk of recidivating and may improve post-release employment odds.
effect_size: -13 percentage points recidivism risk vs non-participants (per rand.org RR-266/RB-9728 landing text)
confidence: cited-in-abstract (OpenAlex abstract + RAND landing page verified)
note: the founder's anchor study; 13pp figure verified on rand.org this run

authors: Robert Bozick, Jennifer Steele, Lois Davis, Heather Turner
title: Does providing inmates with education improve postrelease outcomes? A meta-analysis of correctional education in the United States
key_finding: In highest-caliber research designs, correctional-education participants were 28% less likely to recidivate than non-participants; but participants were AS likely to obtain post-release employment.
effect_size: 28% lower recidivism likelihood (highest-caliber designs); employment effect NULL
note: education→recidivism YES, education→jobs NO: separates the two mechanisms

authors: Neal A. Landenberger, Mark W. Lipsey
title: The positive effects of cognitive-behavioral programs for offenders: a meta-analysis of factors associated with effective treatment
key_finding: Meta-analysis of 58 experimental/quasi-experimental studies confirmed CBT reduces offender recidivism; larger effects with higher-risk offenders, high-quality implementation, and programs including anger control + interpersonal problem solving.
effect_size: positive recidivism reductions confirmed (magnitude not stated in abstract)
note: CBT = the canonical class the founder didn't name: it outperforms all three of his arms in effect density

authors: Mark W. Lipsey, Neal A. Landenberger, Suzanne J. Wilson
title: Effects of Cognitive-Behavioral Programs for Criminal Offenders
key_finding: CBT prevents continuation of criminal careers; implementation quality and well-trained providers matter more than program type or setting (prison vs community made no difference).
effect_size: significant recidivism reductions; no differences by program brand or setting

title: Postsecondary Education Programs Among Incarcerated and Formerly Incarcerated Adults: A Systematic Review of Recidivism Outcomes
venue: Journal of Social Science and Human Research Studies
key_finding: PRISMA-2020 review of 15 studies: postsecondary education is associated with lower recidivism, but the association weakens as methodological rigor increases; strongest for credential completion.
effect_size: positive association; strength diminishes with rigor
note: 2026 sanity-check on the education lane: direction survives, rigor gap flagged

title: The Effects of Prison-Based Educational Programming on Recidivism and Employment
key_finding: Among Minnesota releases 2007-2008: a secondary degree increased odds of post-release employment but had NO significant recidivism effect; a post-secondary degree was associated with more hours worked, higher wages, and less recidivism.
effect_size: post-secondary: less recidivism + higher wages; secondary: employment only, recidivism null
note: level-of-credential matters: splits education into effective vs ineffective variants

title: The Effects of Vocational Education on Recidivism and Employment Among Individuals Released Before and During the COVID-19 Pandemic
venue: International Journal of Offender Therapy and Comparative Criminology
key_finding: Propensity-score-matched evaluation: NO differences in any outcome between vocational-certificate participants and comparison group; prior positive findings attributed to selection bias.
note: the honest-null class: vocational ed effect collapses once selection is controlled

title: Post-release Employment and Recidivism in Norway
key_finding: All 2003 Norwegian prison releases followed monthly (N=7,476): employed ex-inmates show raw recidivism hazard 0.12x, but after adjusting for observable characteristics it is 0.50x — a large share of the employment-recidivism association is selection; residual association persists.
effect_size: raw hazard ratio 0.12 → adjusted 0.50 (p<.001), employment months only
design_class: registry cohort, discrete-time survival, time-varying covariates
note: the definitive honest partial-null for the jobs lane: ~2/3 of the raw effect is selection

title: The Impact of Post-Release Employment on Recidivism in North Carolina
key_finding: 2016 NC prison-exit cohort: early post-release employment is associated with lower 2-year reincarceration; top-quartile earners ~half as likely to be reincarcerated, effect varies sharply by earnings level.
effect_size: top-quartile earnings ≈ 50% lower reincarceration; weaker at low earnings
note: conflict-of-interest flag: working paper, not peer-reviewed venue

authors: Manudeep Bhuller, Gordon B. Dahl, Katrine V. Loken, Magne Mogstad
title: Incarceration, Recidivism and Employment
key_finding: Judge-stringency IV, full Norwegian population panel: incarceration cuts 5-year reoffending by 29pp; the reduction is driven entirely by individuals who were NOT working before incarceration — prison raises program participation, employment, and earnings for them.
effect_size: -29 percentage points reoffending within 5 years; -11 criminal charges; effect concentrated among the previously non-employed
note: the jobs mechanism works THROUGH prison programs, not post-release hiring schemes

title: Evaluating the Minnesota Comprehensive Offender Reentry Plan (MCORP): Results from a Randomized Experiment
key_finding: RCT of a reentry pilot increasing community-service access via improved prison-community case-management collaboration: significantly reduced rearrest, reconviction, and new-offense reincarceration; effects mediated by employment, community support programming (mentoring, restorative justice, faith-based), and social-support systems.
effect_size: significant reductions in all three reoffending types (coefficients not in abstract)
note: the community lane's best causal result: access-to-services + social support, not one service type

title: A randomized experiment of a prisoner reentry program: updated results from an evaluation of the Minnesota Comprehensive Offender Reentry Plan
key_finding: Cox regressions from the same MCORP RCT: significant reductions on 4 of 5 recidivism measures, hazard-ratio reductions of 20-25%; cost-avoidance estimates not robust across assumptions.
note: supplies the quantified effect size the 2011 JQ paper left out

authors: Robert J. Sampson, John H. Laub
title: Crime and Deviance over the Life Course: The Salience of Adult Social Bonds
key_finding: Glueck data reanalysis: despite childhood-delinquency continuity, job stability and strong marital attachment in adulthood inhibit adult criminal behavior — informal social control explains change over the life course.
effect_size: directional (inhibiting); no single effect size in abstract
note: the theoretical base of the community/family lane: work AND marriage bonds, causal tone correlational

title: Transitions from Prison to Community: Understanding Individual Pathways
key_finding: 600,000+ released from state/federal prisons in 2002 (4x the 1975 level); within 3 years almost 7 in 10 rearrested and half returned to prison; reentry pathways are shaped by community-level barriers and supports.
note: scale-setting: why recidivism is a policy target at all
